task: Write one sentence of your own using the word sagacity. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know sagacity should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Her sagacity showed less in what the garden club planted than in what she talked them out of planting.
Sense keeps you from obvious mistakes; sagacity operates far above it, weighing people and years, not just the next step.
Shrewdness is sharp about the deal in front of it, sometimes narrowly so; sagacity is larger - shrewdness plus patience plus the long view.

Wisdom is deep understanding of life and what matters, and it can sit quietly for years without ever being used. Sagacity is wisdom at work: sound judgment applied to a live decision — which offer, which risk — and usually proven right only later.

Judgment is the general faculty of deciding, and the word is neutral: judgment can be hasty, poor, or excellent. Sagacity is a verdict on quality — judgment so keen about people and consequences that time proves it wise.

Prudence is careful judgment aimed at avoiding harm — it counts costs, keeps reserves, and declines the gamble. Sagacity can be bold: its long view sometimes takes the very risk prudence would refuse, because it sees the decade beyond the danger.
foolish misjudgment

Grandpa asked a single question - 'Which boss answered your emails during the interview month?' - and Nia took the smaller offer.
Three years later the startup was gone and her patient employer had tripled her role.
The family started calling Grandpa's question what it was: sagacity.
Sagacity is wisdom applied at decision time - judgment keen about people, patient about consequences, and usually proven right only later.
Cleverness solves the puzzle in front of you; sagacity knows which puzzles are worth solving.
Sagacity is high praise for judgment proven wise over time - the stuff of biographies and case studies.
Its neighbor in this unit, perspicacity, praises the seeing; sagacity praises the deciding.
A scout with perspicacity spots the storm first; a captain with sagacity has already routed around it.

In 1998, superintendent Rosa Maldonado approved what her critics called an outrage: setting fire, on purpose, to four thousand acres of the park she was sworn to protect.
The safe course was obvious — suppress every spark, as the service had for decades.
Her staff urged it; the newspapers demanded it.
Maldonado had read the fuel surveys.
Decades of suppressed fires had loaded the understory with deadwood, and she reasoned that the next lightning strike would find a bomb where a forest should be.
The burn went ahead, ugly and smoky, and cost her a summer of hearings.
Nine years later, when lightning did come, the fire it started ran out of fuel at the old burn line and died.
Rangers there still teach the case as a lesson in sagacity: the long view, held under pressure, proven right by a fire that never grew.
